newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Foreign investors become bullish on Lithuania.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investors become bullish on Lithuania.

text.p: Big-league foreign investors are becoming more bullish on Lithuania's emerging equities market as the country embarks on a concerted drive to complete its economic reforms, senior fund managers said on Tuesday.
"The atmosphere in Lithuania has changed since the new government came to power in the fall," said James Oates, a London-based fund manager for Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS).
Oates was part of a group of foreign investors, which visited Lithuania last week.
"One detects a much more steady commitment to the kinds of reform that have taken place elsewhere in the region," he said.

Lithuania's right-of-centre government, headed by Prime Minister Gediminas Vagnorius, has vowed to sell off key state assets and complete the privatisation process started during his first term of office in 1991-1992.
The government has decided to sell 14 key companies, including the telecommunications company, the airline and other transport firms plus companies in the energy sector.
Fund managers and analysts say that speeding the pace of privatisation is a crucial step to attract foreign capital to the equities market, which has been struggling in recent months.

"The larger companies -- utilities, energy, and communications -- are the ones where big investors will consider putting their money," said Michael Konstantinov, fund manager at Deutsche Investment Trust, part of Dresdner Bank.
The stock market, which has capitalisation of around six billion litas, currently has more than 200 companies quoted but only a fraction of them are active.
"The privatisation process should increase liquidity, which is badly needed in the market right now," he added.
Analysts say the macroeconomic foundations have already been laid for an increased inflow of foreign capital.
"We are positively suprised about how the transition process has been managed in Lithuania and the other Baltic countries," says Konstantinov.
"They are even ahead of some of the central European countries," he said.

Lithuanian shares are also viewed as relatively cheap by funds with central European portfolios and with its northern Baltic neighbour Estonia, where prices have been rising steadily since the share market opened last year.
"Lithuanian shares look quite cheap compared to their peers in central Europe and the other Baltic states," said Oates.
"The quality of the companies is also quite good," he said.
"A significant amount of money should flow into Lithuania...there is lots of room for upward movement on the bourse," he added.
The banking sector, which, in keeping with regional trends, has led the market, is viewed as a potential growth area.
"Some banks should have mark-ups," said Oates.
"We see a lot of consolidation in the banking sector...it is important to monitor who will be the winner," said Konstantinov.
